studies.title: Milk thistle for alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus liver diseases.
studies.abstract: Alcohol and hepatotoxic viruses cause the majority of liver diseases. Randomised clinical trials have assessed whether extracts of milk thistle, Silybum marianum (L) Gaertneri, have any effect in patients with alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus liver diseases. To assess the beneficial and harmful effects of milk thistle or milk thistle constituents versus placebo or no intervention in patients with alcoholic liver disease and/or viral liver diseases (hepatitis B and hepatitis C). The Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and full text searches were combined (July 2007). Manufacturers and researchers in the field were contacted. Only randomised clinical trials in patients with alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus liver diseases (acute and chronic) were included. Interventions encompassed milk thistle at any dose or duration versus placebo or no intervention. The trials could be double blind, single blind, or unblinded. The trials could be unpublished or published and no language limitations were applied. The primary outcome measure was mortality. Binary outcomes are reported as relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). Subgroup analyses were performed with regard to methodological quality. Eighteen randomised clinical trials assessed milk thistle in 1088 patients with alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus liver diseases. The methodological quality was low: only 28.6% of the trials reported high methodological quality characteristics. Milk thistle versus placebo or no intervention had no significant effect on mortality (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.15), complications of liver disease (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.09), or liver histology. Liver-related mortality was significantly reduced by milk thistle in all trials (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.88), but not in high-quality trials (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.19). Milk thistle was not associated with a significantly increased risk of adverse events (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.50). Our results question the beneficial effects of milk thistle for patients with alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus liver diseases and highlight the lack of high-quality evidence to support this intervention. Adequately conducted and reported randomised clinical trials on milk thistle versus placebo are needed.

studies.title: Milk thistle for the treatment of liver disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
studies.abstract: Milk thistle, an herbal compound, is the dietary supplement taken most frequently by patients with chronic liver disease. We performed a systematic review of the literature to determine the efficacy and safety of this herb for the treatment of liver disease. We searched English and non-English reports through July 1999 using thirteen databases and reference lists, and contacting manufacturers and technical experts. Reviewers independently screened all reports to identify randomized placebo-controlled trials that evaluated milk thistle for the treatment of liver disease. Outcomes of primary interest included mortality, histological findings on liver biopsy specimens, serum aminotransferase and albumin levels, and prothrombin times. Fourteen trials met inclusion criteria. Four trials reported outcomes for mortality among 433 participants. The overall summary odds ratio for mortality in the milk thistle group compared with placebo was 0.8 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.5 to 1.5; P = 0.6). Three trials assessed histology on liver biopsy; study quality was inversely associated with the likelihood of histological benefit for milk thistle compared with placebo. There were no differences in serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, or albumin levels, or prothrombin times, among participants assigned to milk thistle compared with those assigned to placebo. The only statistically significant difference was a greater reduction in alanine aminotransferase levels among patients with chronic liver disease assigned to milk thistle (-9 IU/L, 95% CI: -18 to -1 IU/L; P = 0.05), but this reduction was of negligible clinical importance and no longer statistically significant after limiting analyses to studies of longer duration or of higher quality. The frequency of adverse effects was low and, in clinical trials, indistinguishable from placebo. Treatment with milk thistle appears to be safe and well tolerated. We found no reduction in mortality, in improvements in histology at liver biopsy, or in biochemical markers of liver function among patients with chronic liver disease. Data are too limited to exclude a substantial benefit or harm of milk thistle on mortality, and also to support recommending this herbal compound for the treatment of liver disease.

studies.abstract: At present, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) does not have an approved pharmacologic therapy. The present study investigated the protective effects and possible mechanisms of milk thistle ( The NAFLD was established in rats after four weeks of type 2 diabetes induction. The animals were treated with pharmaceutical preparations of milk thistle (Livergol®) and artichoke (Atheromod-B®) extracts for eight weeks. After the end of the intervention, oral glucose tolerance, the serum parameters of oxidative stress, liver functional tests, and lipid profiles were evaluated. Histopathological changes were assessed by hematoxylin and eosin staining. Treatment with preparations of milk thistle and artichoke nonsignificantly improved glucose tolerance in diabetic rats. Both preparations significantly improved serum superoxide dismutase activity and the level of malondialdehyde. Although treatment with milk thistle reduced serum activity of aspartate aminotransferase and serum levels of triglyceride (TG), total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol, artichoke extracts only attenuated the serum level of TG. Milk thistle also effectively protected the liver from histological changes. Milk thistle could be a promising pharmacological option for the treatment of NAFLD. Nonetheless, long-term randomized clinical trials are necessary to confirm the observed results.

studies.title: Transcriptional insights into aflatoxin B1 induced hepatotoxicity and comparative effects of medicinal herbs in pigs.
studies.abstract:
Background

Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) contamination in animal feed poses a serious risk to livestock health due to its hepatotoxic effects. Many medicinal herbs which may be used as feed additives exhibit antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties with potential hepatoprotective outcomes. We investigated effects of AFB1 in three concentrations (30 µg/kg BW, 60 µg/kg BW, 120 µg/kg BW) as well as three medicinal herbs, i.e., kalmegh (Andrographis paniculata), milk thistle (Silybum marianum), and turmeric (Curcuma longa) in pigs. Hepatic expression of genes involved in biotransformation, detoxification, antioxidation, energy homeostasis, and immunity were evaluated by high-throughput real-time PCR.

Results

We found that AFB1 significantly suppressed genes involved in biotransformation (CYP2U1, CYP4V2, CYP7B1, CYP26A1, CYP51A1), detoxification (GSS, ABCC2, SULT1E1), redox balance (GPX1, PRDX4), lipid homeostasis (ACOX1), and immune regulation (CP, CRP). Kalmegh and, to a lesser extent, milk thistle supplementation provided a comprehensive upregulation of genes involved in key hepatic pathways maintaining liver integrity. Under the specific experimental conditions, the applied dietary turmeric supplement did not induce consistent effects on the analyzed target genes.

Conclusions

The results indicate that certain medicinal herbs could counteract AFB1-induced gene expression responses in liver. Their application as dietary supplements to reduce potentially harmful effects caused by AFB1 toxicity in farm animals might be an effective tool in improving animal health, productivity and food safety.

studies.title: Effects of Milk Thistle Extract Supplementation on Performance, Egg Quality, and Liver Pathology of Laying Hens' Fed Diets Lacking Supplemental Choline Chloride
studies.abstract: The current study evaluated the effects of milk thistle extract supplementation in laying hens' fed diets lacking choline chloride addition. A total of 60 Isa-brown laying hens were randomly allocated into T1: control diet, 0% extract supplementation; T2: control diet with 1% extract; T3: control diet with 2.5% extract; and T4: control diet with 4% extract. Egg quality parameters, yolk lipid oxidation, malondialdehyde (MDA) content, and fatty acid profile were assessed. Livers were examined grossly and histologically to evaluate hepatocellular lesions such as vacuolization (lipidosis), reticular stromal architecture, the amount of collagenous connective tissue, and vascular wall changes. Groups T3 and T4 showed darker yolks compared to both control group and T2 (p = 0.001) and redness of the egg yolk (p < 0.001). The MDA was lowest in T2 group which had improved gross appearance with lower degrees of hepatic vacuolization than other groups. Liver discoloration was milder in T3 (43.8%) compared to the T1 and T4 groups (18.8% and 12.5%, respectively, p = 0.013). Reticulin loss was correlated with the degree of hepatic vacuolization (r = 0.751, p < 0.001). Supplementation with MT extract in diets lacking choline chloride may influence certain egg quality indices and liver gross macroscopic lesions in laying hens.

studies.title: Feasible feeding strategies for sustainable management of serve heat stress conditions: Effect of Milk Thistle extract on growth performance and health status o
studies.abstract: The trail aimed to explore the effect of dietary supplementation of Milk Thistle (MT) extract on growth performance and health status of growing rabbits exposed to serve heat stress condition, considering the economic efficiency of supplementation. A total of 96 weaned male rabbits were divided into 4 groups (24 rabbits/group). The first group received the basal diet without any supplementation and served as a control (MT0), while 2nd, 3rd and 4th groups supplemented with MT at levels of 5 (MT5), 10 (MT10) and 15 (MT15) g/kg diet, respectively, for 10 consecutive weeks. Both of growth performance and feed utilisation were significantly enhanced by the dietary treatment, the optimum dose of MT was 12 g/kg diet for average daily gain, specific growth rate and performance index. However, it was 13 g/kg diet for feed conversation ratio. The polynomial regression analysis showed that the lowest values of rectal temperature and respiration rate were observed at doses of 11 and 13 g/kg diet respectively. The dressing percentage and the relative weights of liver and total edible giblets were significantly improved by the treatment (p = 0.0416, 0.0112 and 0.0032, respectively), maximising in the MT10 group. The MT10 and MT15 groups showed higher erythrocytes and leucocytes counts and lower levels of urea, creatinine and total cholesterol compared to the control (p < 0.05). Liver functions significantly enhanced in aforementioned two treated groups, the liver ultrastructure represented normal cytoplasmic organelles, and nucleus and mitochondria in MT10 group, while the MT15 group showed hepatocytes with dilated nucleus with most cytoplasmic organelles appeared well organised and normal except few small cytoplasms vacuolated. The levels glutathione, superoxide dismutase, catalase and total antioxidant capacity as well as immunoglobulin M, and immunoglobulin G significant improved in the MT-Treated groups compared to the control (p < 0.05). Economically, MT supplemented diets improved the net revenue of fattened rabbits during the summer season. In conclusion, the supplementation of MT extract at levels of 10 or 15 g/kg diet enhanced growth performance, feed utilisation, dressing percentage, hemato-biochemical attributes, immunity and redox balance of heat stressed growing rabbits during the hot season.

studies.title: Milk thistle nano-micelle formulation promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma cells through modulating miR-155-3p /SOCS2 /PHLDA1 si
studies.abstract: Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is a prevalent form of liver cancer that causes significant mortality in numerous individuals worldwide. This study compared the effects of milk thistle (MT) and nano-milk thistle (N-MT) on the expression of the genes that participate in apoptosis and cell cycle pathways in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells. IC50 values of MT and N-MT were determined using the MTT assay. Huh-7 and HepG2 cell lines (containing mutant and wild-type TP53 gene, respectively) were incubated with MT and N-MT for 24h and 48h and the impact of MT and N-MT on the proliferation of these cell lines was evaluated through a comparative analysis. Cell cycle and apoptosis were assessed by flow cytometry after 24h and 48h treatment in the cell lines mentioned. Real-time PCR was used to analyze miR-155-3p, PHLDA1, SOCS2, TP53, P21, BAX, and BCL-2 expression in the cell lines that were being treated. N-MT reduces cancer cell growth in a time and concentration-dependent manner, which is more toxic compared to MT. Huh-7 was observed to have IC50 values of 2.35 and 1.7 μg/ml at 24h and 48h, and HepG2 was observed to have IC50 values of 3.4 and 2.6 μg/ml at 24 and 48h, respectively. N-MT arrested Huh-7 and HepG2 cells in the Sub-G1 phase and induced apoptosis. N-MT led to a marked reduction in the expression of miR-155-3p and BCL-2 after 24h and 48h treatments. Conversely, PHLDA1, SOCS2, BAX, and P21 were upregulated in the treated cells compared to untreated cells, which suggests that milk thistle has the potential to regulate these genes. N-MT reduced the expression of TP53 in Huh-7 cells after mentioned time points, while there was a significant increase in the expression of the TP53 gene in HepG2 cells. No gene expression changes were observed in MT-treated cells after 24h and 48h. N-MT can regulate cancer cell death by arresting cell cycle and inducing apoptosis. This occurs through the alteration of apoptotic genes expression. A reduction in the expression of miR-155-3p and increase in the expression of SOCS2 and PHLDA1 after N-MT treatment showed the correlation between miR-155-3p and PHLDA1/SOCS2 found in bioinformatics analysis. While N-MT increased TP53 expression in HepG2, reduced it in Huh-7. The findings indicate that N-MT can function intelligently in cancer cells and can be a helpful complement to cancer treatment.

studies.title: Effect of Milk Thistle (Silybum marianum) Supplementation on Pork Offal Quality.
studies.abstract: The aim of the study was to determine the effect of milk thistle supplementation of fattener pig feeds on physical and chemical properties of pork offal. The experiments were conducted on 60 fatteners (group C-control (30 pigs) and group E-experimental (30 pigs)). The experimental group was supplemented with ground milk thistle (Silybum marianum) at 7 g/kg feed. The offal (tongues, kidneys, hearts, lungs and livers) was analyzed for weight, pH, WHC, water, protein, fat, energy value, fatty acid profile and content of major and trace elements. The present study shows that milk thistle added to fattener pig diets increased pH45 and pH24 values in most of the analyzed offal and significantly (p ≤ 0.01) decreased the weight of heart and lungs and increased the weight of liver and kidneys. Hearts, lungs and kidneys of the experimental group contained more fat and the liver less, than the same offal of the control group. As regards the content of elements, the dietary supplement most often had an effect on the heart and lungs. In general, milk thistle supplemented in fattener diets had modified the physical parameters and chemical composition of the analyzed products.

studies.title: Effect of Milk Thistle (Silybum marianum) Seed Cakes by Horses Subjected to Physical Exertion
studies.abstract: Milk thistle (Silybum marianum) provides several possible benefits for horses, namely anti–inflammatory, antioxidant effects, hepatoprotective, and neuroprotective effects. Silybin exerts also pronounced effects on energy metabolism, that could be useful for sport horses. The aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of milk thistle seed cakes (in the form of a granulated mixture with barley) on blood biochemical parameters (total protein, albumin, bilirubin, urea, creatinine, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, LDH, the total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, TAG, BHB, NEFA, creatine kinase, lactate, glucose, glutathione peroxidase, total antioxidant capacity, cortisol, calcium, and phosphorus) to monitor the differences between the experimental (milk thistle in feed) and control horses after exposure of the monitored horses to heavy physical exercise (combined driving) total number of horses was 12 Czech Warmblood breed horses. The digestibility of silymarin (and its individual flavonolignans) and basic nutrients are also monitored in this study. Statistically significant differences (P < .05) were found mainly in plasma cortisol and NEFA levels. The results of this study confirmed the results of our previous studies. These results suggest that the feeding of milk thistle seed cakes has a possible positive effect on horse health and energy metabolism.

studies.title: Treatment with milk thistle extract (Silybum marianum), ursodeoxycholic acid, or their combination attenuates cholestatic liver injury in rats: Role of the hepa
studies.abstract: Cholestasis, which results in hepatic cell death, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventually liver failure, is associated with oxidative stress. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of milk thistle (MT, Silybum marianum) and ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) or their combination on the activation of hepatic stem cells and on the severity of cholestasis liver injury in rats. Under anesthesia, bile ducts of female Sprague Dawley rats were ligated (BDL) or had sham operation. BDL rats were administered saline, UDCA (15 mg/kg/d), MT (600 mg/kg/d), or UDCA+MT by gavage for 10 days. On the 11th day, rats were sacrificed and blood and liver samples were obtained. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), hepatic malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) activity were measured. Hepatic injury, a-smooth muscle actin expression, and stem cell markers c-kit, c-Myc, Oct3/4, and SSEA-1 were histologically determined. Histological scores, serum ALT, and hepatic MDA levels were higher in BDL group than in the sham rats, while all treatments significantly reduced these levels. The reduction in ALT was significantly greater in UCDA+MT-treated group than in other treatment groups. c-Kit, c-Myc, Oct3/4, and SSEA-1 were increased in saline-treated BDL group with respect to sham-operated control group, and these markers were significantly reduced in all treatment groups. In addition to a modulatory effect on the stem cell-induced regenerative response of the liver, UDCA, MT, and their combination demonstrated similar anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative effects on cholestasis-induced hepatic injury.

studies.title: Fermented goat milk enriched with milk thistle seed powder and its bioactive compounds: Chemical composition, color, texture, antioxidant activity, microbial qu
studies.abstract: Due to its superior antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, milk thistle has been widely used in various applications. In the present study, the effects of milk thistle seeds (MTS) powder and its ethanolic bioactive compounds extract on fermented goat milk were investigated. Fresh goat milk was enriched with 0.5%, 1%, and 2% of MTS powder and its extract, and the obtained product was analyzed after 1 and 14 d of cold storage. The MTS bioactive compound-ethanolic extract displayed higher antioxidant activities (DPPH•, ABTS•<sup>+</sup>, and ferric reducing antioxidant power) and total phenolic compounds compared with those extracted by using homogenization, ultrasonication, or microwave. The fatty acid composition analysis of MTS oil revealed that linoleic, oleic, palmitic, and stearic were the predominant fatty acids. The results also show that the addition of MTS significantly affected different yogurt characteristics. The MTS extract-enriched samples had higher moisture content than MTS powder-enriched and the control samples. Yogurt color, texture, and volatile compound profile were also influenced by the inclusion of MTS into yogurt formulation. The control yogurt samples displayed higher levels of 2,3-butanedione, 2-heptanone, 3-hydroxy-2-butanone, and 2-nonanone. In addition, MTS enhanced the antioxidant activities and microbial quality of goat milk yogurt.

studies.title: Effects of Different Forms of Milk Thistle Supplementation in Rabbit Diets on Stress-Induced Physiological Responses.
studies.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of thermal and noise stress on rabbits (90 HYLA hybrids), focusing on physiological responses, production performance, and welfare. Three dietary treatments were compared: a control diet (C), a diet supplemented with milk thistle seed cake (SMT), and a diet containing fermented milk thistle seed cake (FMT). The aim was to assess whether these feed additives could mitigate the adverse effects of environmental stress. Health status was monitored through clinical observation and analysis of biochemical indicators, including enzymes, lipid and protein metabolism markers, and total antioxidant status. Thermal stress at the onset of fattening influenced average daily gain, feed intake, and carcass yield, while dietary intervention modulated these effects. The FMT group demonstrated the lowest feed intake and most efficient feed conversion during later growth stages, but had lower slaughter weight compared with the control. In contrast, rabbits fed the SMT diet achieved the highest slaughter weight and superior growth efficiency. These findings suggest that milk thistle, particularly in combination with probiotic fermentation, can enhance feed utilization, growth performance, and stress resilience in rabbits, contributing to more sustainable and welfare-oriented production systems.

studies.title: Semen quality, antioxidant status and reproductive performance of rabbits bucks fed milk thistle seeds and rosemary leaves.
studies.abstract: The study aimed to investigate the effects of milk thistle seeds (MTS) and rosemary leaves (RL) both at 5 and 10g/kg diet on reproductive performance, semen quality and blood metabolites of rabbit bucks. A total of 35 rabbit bucks were randomly distributed into five experimental groups (7 bucks/group). All the groups were fed the same basal diet. The 1st group (control) did not have MTS and RL in its basal diet. The 2nd and 3rd groups were supplemented with MTS at 5 and 10g/kg, respectively. The 4th and 5th groups were fed the basal diet supplemented with RL at 5 and 10g/kg, respectively. The sperm concentration (SC), total sperm output (TSO), live sperm (LS), total live sperm (TLS) and total motile sperm (TMS) were significantly greater in the bucks fed MTS at 10 and RL at 5g/kg diet than the control group. Bucks fed MTS at 10g/kg diet had higher fertility than the control. Also, RL 5g/kg group showed higher testosterone and fertility than the control, but the MTS 10g/kg group showed the highest value for both parameters. In conclusion, MTS and RL at 10 and 5g/kg, respectively, significantly improved the semen quality and the fertility and MTS also increased the economic efficiency of rabbit bucks.

Yogurt color, texture, and volatile compound profile were also influenced by the inclusion of MTS into yogurt formulation. The control yogurt samples displayed higher levels of 2,3-butanedione, 2-heptanone, 3-hydroxy-2-butanone, and 2-nonanone. In addition, MTS enhanced the antioxidant activities and microbial quality of goat milk yogurt.

studies.title: Transcriptional insights into aflatoxin B1 induced hepatotoxicity and comparative effects of medicinal herbs in pigs.
studies.abstract:
Background

Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) contamination in animal feed poses a serious risk to livestock health due to its hepatotoxic effects. Many medicinal herbs which may be used as feed additives exhibit antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties with potential hepatoprotective outcomes. We investigated effects of AFB1 in three concentrations (30 µg/kg BW, 60 µg/kg BW, 120 µg/kg BW) as well as three medicinal herbs, i.e., kalmegh (Andrographis paniculata), milk thistle (Silybum marianum), and turmeric (Curcuma longa) in pigs. Hepatic expression of genes involved in biotransformation, detoxification, antioxidation, energy homeostasis, and immunity were evaluated by high-throughput real-time PCR.

Results

We found that AFB1 significantly suppressed genes involved in biotransformation (CYP2U1, CYP4V2, CYP7B1, CYP26A1, CYP51A1), detoxification (GSS, ABCC2, SULT1E1), redox balance (GPX1, PRDX4), lipid homeostasis (ACOX1), and immune regulation (CP, CRP). Kalmegh and, to a lesser extent, milk thistle supplementation provided a comprehensive upregulation of genes involved in key hepatic pathways maintaining liver integrity. Under the specific experimental conditions, the applied dietary turmeric supplement did not induce consistent effects on the analyzed target genes.

Conclusions

The results indicate that certain medicinal herbs could counteract AFB1-induced gene expression responses in liver. Their application as dietary supplements to reduce potentially harmful effects caused by AFB1 toxicity in farm animals might be an effective tool in improving animal health, productivity and food safety.

studies.title: Effect of milk thistle (Silybum marianum L.) oil on pro-inflammatory cytokines, acute phase proteins, rumen metagenomic profile, rumen fluid variables and perfo
studies.abstract: The aim of this study was to determine the effect of milk thistle (Silybum marianum L., SM) oil supplementation on proinflammatory cytokines, acute phase proteins, rumen metagenomic profile, rumen fluid variables and performance during the milk feeding period of Holstein calves. In the present study, 24 calves that consumed quality and sufficient amount of colostrum (≥50 mg/ml IgG) after birth were divided into three groups, with 8 animals in each group (4 males + 4 females). Individually fed calves were given added SM oil as 0 µL/day/calf (Control group, SM0), 100 µL/day/calf (SM100) and 200 µL/day/calf (SM200). The ration containing concentrated feed mix (90%) + wheat straw (10%) was offered to the calves. SM oil did not change the ammonia nitrogen and pH values of the rumen fluid of calf (P>0.05). The molarities of PA, IBA, IVA and BSCFA in the rumen fluid increased linearly with SM oil dose (P<0.05). The relative abundance of Firmicutes linearly increased and the relative abundance of Actinobacteriota decreased with the addition of SM oil (P<0.05). Relative abundances of Erysipelotrichaceae_UCG_002, Eubacterium_coprostanoligenes_group, Clostridia_UCG_014, Lachnospiraceae_Unknown_1, Lachnospiraceae_NK3A20_group, Shuttleworthia, Selenomonadaceae_Uncultured_1, Rikenellaceae_RC9_gut_group and Succinivibrionaceae_UCG_001 linearly increased with SM oil (P<0.05). Relative abundances of Methanobrevibacter, Acetitomaculum, Olsenella and Megasphaera in calf rumen fluid linearly decreased with SM oil (P<0.05). Concentrations of TNF-α, IFN-ɣ, and SAA of calf' serum at weaning stage linearly decreased with SM oil doses (P<0.05). Serum IgA concentration increased with 100 µL SM oil /day (P<0.05). As a result, the addition of SM oil to calves has the potential to reduce the immune suppression of calves during the milk feeding period and at weaning time, has a positive effect on the microbiome involved in starch and protein catabolism in the rumen fluid, and increases the fermentation end products (PA, IVA and BA). Milk thistle oil has an inhibitory effect on methanogenic archaea and can be used as an anti-methanogenic feed additive and will contribute to the effective use of feed energy.

studies.title: Effect of Milk Thistle (Silybum marianum) Seed Cakes by Horses Subjected to Physical Exertion
studies.abstract: Milk thistle (Silybum marianum) provides several possible benefits for horses, namely anti–inflammatory, antioxidant effects, hepatoprotective, and neuroprotective effects. Silybin exerts also pronounced effects on energy metabolism, that could be useful for sport horses. The aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of milk thistle seed cakes (in the form of a granulated mixture with barley) on blood biochemical parameters (total protein, albumin, bilirubin, urea, creatinine, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, LDH, the total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, TAG, BHB, NEFA, creatine kinase, lactate, glucose, glutathione peroxidase, total antioxidant capacity, cortisol, calcium, and phosphorus) to monitor the differences between the experimental (milk thistle in feed) and control horses after exposure of the monitored horses to heavy physical exercise (combined driving) total number of horses was 12 Czech Warmblood breed horses. The digestibility of silymarin (and its individual flavonolignans) and basic nutrients are also monitored in this study. Statistically significant differences (P < .05) were found mainly in plasma cortisol and NEFA levels. The results of this study confirmed the results of our previous studies. These results suggest that the feeding of milk thistle seed cakes has a possible positive effect on horse health and energy metabolism.

studies.title: Treatment with milk thistle extract (Silybum marianum), ursodeoxycholic acid, or their combination attenuates cholestatic liver injury in rats: Role of the hepa
studies.abstract: Cholestasis, which results in hepatic cell death, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventually liver failure, is associated with oxidative stress. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of milk thistle (MT, Silybum marianum) and ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) or their combination on the activation of hepatic stem cells and on the severity of cholestasis liver injury in rats. Under anesthesia, bile ducts of female Sprague Dawley rats were ligated (BDL) or had sham operation. BDL rats were administered saline, UDCA (15 mg/kg/d), MT (600 mg/kg/d), or UDCA+MT by gavage for 10 days. On the 11th day, rats were sacrificed and blood and liver samples were obtained. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), hepatic malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) activity were measured. Hepatic injury, a-smooth muscle actin expression, and stem cell markers c-kit, c-Myc, Oct3/4, and SSEA-1 were histologically determined. Histological scores, serum ALT, and hepatic MDA levels were higher in BDL group than in the sham rats, while all treatments significantly reduced these levels. The reduction in ALT was significantly greater in UCDA+MT-treated group than in other treatment groups. c-Kit, c-Myc, Oct3/4, and SSEA-1 were increased in saline-treated BDL group with respect to sham-operated control group, and these markers were significantly reduced in all treatment groups. In addition to a modulatory effect on the stem cell-induced regenerative response of the liver, UDCA, MT, and their combination demonstrated similar anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative effects on cholestasis-induced hepatic injury.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Herbal extract from milk thistle plant; traditional remedy for liver support
explanation.what_it_is: Milk thistle is a plant (Silybum marianum) native to the Mediterranean. The active compound is silymarin, a mixture of flavonolignans — molecules that plants make naturally — extracted from the plant's seeds. People typically take it as a capsule, tablet, or liquid extract.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Acts as an antioxidant; reduces cellular damage from harmful free radicals
explanation.how_it_works: Milk thistle contains silymarin, which works like a cellular cleanup crew. Free radicals are unstable oxygen molecules that damage cells; silymarin neutralizes them before they can cause harm — a process called antioxidation. It also appears to support liver cells' own repair systems and may reduce inflammatory signals (cytokines — proteins cells use to communicate inflammation). The exact pathways are still being mapped, but the antioxidant effect is well-established in test tubes and animal models.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in short-term human trials; long-term and population-specific safety unclear
explanation.safety_detail: The meta-analyses and human studies retrieved reported few adverse events over their study periods (typically weeks to months), with milk thistle generally tolerated as well as placebo. However, the retrieved trials involved small populations and short durations; safety over years, or in people with specific medical conditions, has not been adequately tested in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Pregnancy and lactation: not tested in retrieved human trials — safety unknown
Kidney or severe liver disease: excluded from most trials — untested in these populations
Drug interactions: not systematically assessed in the records provided; silymarin may affect liver enzymes that metabolize medications
explanation.chem_meaning: Silymarin is a large, plant-derived polyphenol molecule — bulky and polar (water-loving), so it dissolves poorly in plain water but is often extracted in alcohol or made into specialized formulations to improve absorption. This chemistry explains why it is not easily absorbed from the gut, which is one reason efficacy in humans may be lower than animal studies suggest.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses from 2002, 2005, and 2007 combined human data from over 2000 participants with alcoholic liver disease, hepatitis B, or hepatitis C. The pooled effect shows a modest reduction in disease risk (risk ratio 0.78, meaning about 22% lower risk compared to control), though the confidence interval is wide (0.53–1.15) and includes the possibility of no effect. Recent animal studies (2022–2026) confirm silymarin reduces liver damage from toxins in chickens and other models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four human studies exist, but all are meta-analyses of older trials rather than new primary studies; this limits the strength of evidence. The pooled result is modest and imprecise, and most individual trial sample sizes were small by modern standards, so confidence is capped at Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single animal study (2022) tested silibinin (the main compound in milk thistle) in rodents exposed to formaldehyde, a neurotoxin. The compound reduced oxidative stress in brain tissue and improved cognitive function in that model.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one animal study exists; no human trials have tested milk thistle or silibinin for cognition. Animal findings do not reliably translate to humans, so this remains preliminary and unproven in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three animal studies (2017, 2025, 2026) examined milk thistle in rabbits under stress or as a dietary supplement. They reported improvements in semen quality, sperm motility, and reproductive hormone markers, likely via the antioxidant effect reducing testicular damage.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is in animals; no human studies of milk thistle and sexual function were retrieved. Animal models cannot be assumed to predict human outcomes, so this remains preliminary.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human study (2022, unclassified design and small, sample size not verified in the abstract) reported anti-inflammatory effects. Eight animal studies (2022–2026) in various species (rodents, chickens, rabbits) consistently showed reductions in pro-inflammatory cytokines (signaling molecules that drive inflammation) and acute-phase proteins (markers of inflammation in the blood).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only a single, small human study addresses this; no consistency can be assessed across independent human evidence. Precision is also unclear because sample sizes could not be verified from abstracts. Animal data are supportive but do not confirm efficacy in people.

explanation.evidence_base: Evidence is mixed: liver health rests on four human meta-analyses from clinical trials conducted in the 1990s–2000s, involving over 2000 total participants with viral or alcoholic liver disease, so human evidence exists but is dated and of modest quality. Cognition, sexual function, and inflammation are supported only by animal studies from 2017 onward, which cannot reliably predict human outcomes. The overall moderate tier for the compound reflects the liver data; outcomes beyond liver are preliminary and unproven in humans.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records do not include primary human trials designed in recent years for any outcome, which raises the question of whether newer, larger, and better-controlled studies have been conducted but are not represented here. Within the records: cognition, sexual function, and inflammation lack human evidence entirely. Liver health evidence is older (pre-2010) and involves small, heterogeneous trials; whether milk thistle helps in modern clinical practice remains uncertain. Long-term safety (beyond months) and efficacy in people with kidney disease, severe liver impairment, or pregnant women have not been adequately tested in the provided studies.

appraisal.headline: Liver health evidence rests entirely on three meta-analyses from 2002–2007 with a pooled confidence interval spanning zero (0.53–1.15), and the remaining outcomes rely on animal models with no human replication.

concerns.issue: Pooled effect includes null; all human liver evidence is secondary
concerns.detail: The liver health outcome—the strongest in this evidence base—shows a pooled risk ratio of 0.78 [0.53–1.15], where the confidence interval crosses 1.0, meaning the effect is statistically indistinguishable from no effect. Critically, all human evidence consists of only 3 meta-analyses (2002, 2005, 2007); no primary human trials are present in the retrieved records. The engine explicitly notes 'Limited human evidence: 0 primary human studies.' This means the grade rests on secondary synthesis of older primary trials, not direct observation of milk thistle's efficacy in humans.

concerns.issue: Three non-liver outcomes have zero human trials
concerns.detail: Cognition, sexual function, and inflammation are each graded as Preliminary, and the records show cognition has 1 animal study only, sexual function has 3 animal studies, and inflammation has only 1 unclassified human study alongside 8 animal studies. No human randomized controlled trials or observational studies appear in the retrieved evidence for these outcomes. Animal toxicology or performance models (e.g., formaldehyde-induced cognitive impairment in rodents, semen quality in rabbits) do not reliably predict human outcomes.

concerns.issue: Sample size transparency severely limited; most abstracts omit n
concerns.detail: Of 13 liver health studies, only 5 report sample sizes in the abstracts (60, 96, 433, 915, 1088). The engine notes 'most abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is substantially larger,' meaning the precision estimate of ~2592 verified participants is a lower bound and potentially masks heterogeneity in study quality or size. For inflammation (9 studies), sample sizes could not be extracted from abstracts at all, capping precision assessment. For sexual function, only 1 of 3 animal studies reports n=35, leaving two studies entirely undocumented for rigor evaluation.

concerns.issue: Meta-analyses are 15–22 years old; primary trial base is unknown
concerns.detail: The three meta-analyses pooling human evidence date to 2002, 2005, and 2007. No newer human meta-analysis or primary trial is present in the retrieved records, raising the possibility that the underlying primary trials may be even older or that more recent evidence is not represented. Without access to the primary studies cited in those meta-analyses, it is impossible to assess their individual quality, population specificity (e.g., only hepatitis B/C and alcohol-induced liver disease), or whether results apply to general liver health.

concerns.issue: Inflammation outcome lacks quantifiable pooled effect; consistency unassessable
concerns.detail: The inflammation outcome is graded Preliminary, and the engine explicitly notes 'no pooled effect extractable' and 'only one human study addresses this outcome; consistency cannot be assessed across independent human evidence.' With 8 of 9 studies being animal models and only 1 unclassified human study, there is no basis for inferring human-relevant inflammatory benefit, and no replication exists to test reproducibility.

appraisal.mechanism_check: The proposed mechanism—silymarin or silibinin exerts hepatoprotective effects via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways—is plausible in isolated cells and animal toxicology models (e.g., aflatoxin B1 hepatotoxicity in rodents, formaldehyde-induced cognitive impairment). However, there is a large inferential leap from animal liver injury models to human liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis, or general metabolic health): animal studies use acute toxin exposure or stress, while human liver disease is chronic and multifactorial. The pooled human evidence (meta-analyses of 2002–2007) does not provide mechanistic data—only clinical endpoints—and the confidence interval spans zero, leaving even the clinical relevance of the mechanism unconfirmed.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would argue that the 'Moderate' grade for liver health is overstated: the pooled effect (RR 0.78 [0.53–1.15]) is not statistically significant, the evidence base consists only of three 15–22-year-old meta-analyses with unknown underlying trial quality, and those meta-analyses focused narrowly on alcoholic and viral hepatitis liver disease, not general liver health. The non-liver outcomes (cognition, sexual function, inflammation) rest entirely on animal models in rabbits, horses, rodents, and poultry—populations and disease models remote from human clinical use—with zero replication in humans. Taken together, the evidence base does not support claims of clinical benefit in humans beyond a possible signal in a narrow hepatitis/alcohol subpopulation that may be outdated.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A high-quality, adequately powered (n ≥ 200) double-blind randomized controlled trial in humans with a specific liver disease (e.g., non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis, or drug-induced liver injury) using standardized milk thistle extract, measured liver function tests and fibrosis markers as primary outcomes, and published in the past 5 years would substantially clarify human efficacy. Parallel replication of the same design in an independent population would further establish reproducibility and applicability.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Extracto herbal de la planta de cardo de leche; remedio tradicional para el apoyo hepático
explanation_es.what_it_is: El cardo de leche es una planta (Silybum marianum) nativa del Mediterráneo. El compuesto activo es la silimarina, una mezcla de flavonolignanos —moléculas que las plantas producen naturalmente— extraída de las semillas de la planta. Las personas típicamente la toman como cápsula, tableta o extracto líquido.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Actúa como antioxidante; reduce el daño celular causado por radicales libres perjudiciales
explanation_es.how_it_works: El cardo de leche contiene silimarina, que funciona como un equipo de limpieza celular. Los radicales libres son moléculas de oxígeno inestables que dañan las células; la silimarina las neutraliza antes de que puedan causar daño —un proceso llamado antioxidación. También parece apoyar los propios sistemas de reparación de las células hepáticas y puede reducir las señales inflamatorias (citoquinas —proteínas que las células utilizan para comunicar inflamación). Las vías exactas aún se están mapeando, pero el efecto antioxidante está bien establecido en tubos de ensayo y modelos animales.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerado en ensayos humanos a corto plazo; la seguridad a largo plazo y específica de poblaciones es incierta
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los metanálisis y estudios humanos recuperados reportaron pocos eventos adversos durante sus períodos de estudio (típicamente semanas a meses), siendo el cardo de leche generalmente tolerado tan bien como el placebo. Sin embargo, los ensayos recuperados involucraron poblaciones pequeñas y duraciones cortas; la seguridad a lo largo de años, o en personas con condiciones médicas específicas, no ha sido adecuadamente probada en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Embarazo y lactancia: no probado en ensayos humanos recuperados — seguridad desconocida
Enfermedad renal o hepática grave: excluido de la mayoría de ensayos — no probado en estas poblaciones
Interacciones medicamentosas: no evaluado sistemáticamente en los registros proporcionados; la silimarina puede afectar las enzimas hepáticas que metabolizan medicamentos
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La silimarina es una molécula polifenol grande derivada de plantas —voluminosa e hidrófila (amante del agua)— por lo que se disuelve mal en agua pura pero frecuentemente se extrae en alcohol o se formula en formas especializadas para mejorar la absorción. Esta química explica por qué no se absorbe fácilmente desde el intestino, lo cual es una razón por la que la eficacia en humanos puede ser menor de lo que sugieren los estudios animales.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Metanálisis de 2002, 2005 y 2007 combinaron datos humanos de más de 2000 participantes con enfermedad hepática alcohólica, hepatitis B o hepatitis C. El efecto agrupado muestra una reducción modesta en el riesgo de enfermedad (razón de riesgo 0.78, significando aproximadamente 22% menor riesgo comparado con control), aunque el intervalo de confianza es amplio (0.53–1.15) e incluye la posibilidad de ausencia de efecto. Estudios animales recientes (2022–2026) confirman que la silimarina reduce el daño hepático causado por toxinas en pollos y otros modelos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen cuatro estudios humanos, pero todos son metanálisis de ensayos más antiguos en lugar de nuevos estudios primarios; esto limita la solidez de la evidencia. El resultado agrupado es modesto e impreciso, y la mayoría de los tamaños de muestra de ensayos individuales fueron pequeños según estándares modernos, por lo que la confianza se limita a Moderada en lugar de Fuerte.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un único estudio animal (2022) probó silibinina (el compuesto principal en el cardo de leche) en roedores expuestos a formaldehído, una neurotoxina. El compuesto redujo el estrés oxidativo en el tejido cerebral y mejoró la función cognitiva en ese modelo.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo existe un estudio animal; ningún ensayo humano ha probado el cardo de leche o silibinina para la cognición. Los hallazgos animales no se traducen confiablemente a humanos, por lo que esto sigue siendo preliminar y no probado en personas.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Tres estudios animales (2017, 2025, 2026) examinaron el cardo de leche en conejos bajo estrés o como suplemento dietético. Reportaron mejoras en la calidad del semen, motilidad de espermatozoides y marcadores de hormonas reproductivas, probablemente a través del efecto antioxidante reduciendo el daño testicular.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Toda la evidencia es en animales; ningún estudio humano del cardo de leche y función sexual fue recuperado. Los modelos animales no pueden asumirse que predigan resultados humanos, por lo que esto sigue siendo preliminar.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un estudio humano (2022, diseño no clasificado y pequeño, tamaño de muestra no verificado en el resumen) reportó efectos antiinflamatorios. Ocho estudios animales (2022–2026) en varias especies (roedores, pollos, conejos) mostraron consistentemente reducciones en citoquinas proinflamatorias (moléculas de señalización que impulsan la inflamación) y proteínas de fase aguda (marcadores de inflamación en la sangre).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo un único estudio humano pequeño aborda esto; no puede evaluarse consistencia entre evidencia humana independiente. La precisión también es incierta porque los tamaños de muestra no pudieron verificarse desde resúmenes. Los datos animales son de apoyo pero no confirman eficacia en personas.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia es mixta: la salud hepática descansa en cuatro metanálisis humanos de ensayos clínicos realizados en los años 1990–2000, involucrando más de 2000 participantes totales con enfermedad hepática viral o alcohólica, por lo que existe evidencia humana pero es antigua y de calidad modesta. Cognición, función sexual e inflamación son soportadas solo por estudios animales de 2017 en adelante, que no pueden predecir confiablemente resultados humanos. El nivel moderado general para el compuesto refleja los datos hepáticos; los resultados más allá del hígado son preliminares y no probados en humanos.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados no incluyen ensayos humanos primarios diseñados en años recientes para ningún resultado, lo que plantea la pregunta de si estudios más nuevos, más grandes y mejor controlados han sido realizados pero no están representados aquí. Dentro de los registros: cognición, función sexual e inflamación carecen completamente de evidencia humana. La evidencia de salud hepática es más antigua (anterior a 2010) e involucra ensayos pequeños y heterogéneos; si el cardo de leche ayuda en la práctica clínica moderna sigue siendo incierto. La seguridad a largo plazo (más allá de meses) y eficacia en personas con enfermedad renal, insuficiencia hepática grave, o mujeres embarazadas no han sido adecuadamente probadas en los estudios proporcionados.

appraisal_es.headline: La evidencia de salud hepática descansa enteramente en tres metanálisis de 2002–2007 con un intervalo de confianza agrupado que abarca cero (0.53–1.15), y los resultados restantes se basan en modelos animales sin replicación en humanos.

concerns.issue: El efecto agrupado incluye la nulidad; toda la evidencia hepática humana es secundaria
concerns.detail: El resultado de salud hepática—el más fuerte en esta base de evidencia—muestra un cociente de riesgos agrupado de 0.78 [0.53–1.15], donde el intervalo de confianza cruza 1.0, lo que significa que el efecto es estadísticamente indistinguible de la ausencia de efecto. De manera crítica, toda la evidencia humana consiste únicamente en 3 metanálisis (2002, 2005, 2007); no hay ensayos humanos primarios presentes en los registros recuperados. El motor explícitamente señala 'Evidencia humana limitada: 0 estudios humanos primarios.' Esto significa que la calificación descansa en síntesis secundaria de ensayos primarios antiguos, no en observación directa de la eficacia del cardo mariano en humanos.

concerns.issue: Tres resultados no hepáticos tienen cero ensayos en humanos
concerns.detail: Cognición, función sexual e inflamación están cada uno calificados como Preliminares, y los registros muestran que cognición tiene solo 1 estudio animal, función sexual tiene 3 estudios animales e inflamación tiene solo 1 estudio humano sin clasificar junto con 8 estudios animales. No aparecen ensayos controlados aleatorizados en humanos ni estudios observacionales en la evidencia recuperada para estos resultados. Los modelos de toxicología animal o rendimiento (p. ej., deterioro cognitivo inducido por formaldehído en roedores, calidad del semen en conejos) no predicen de manera confiable los resultados en humanos.

concerns.issue: La transparencia del tamaño de muestra es severamente limitada; la mayoría de resúmenes omiten n
concerns.detail: De 13 estudios de salud hepática, solo 5 reportan tamaños de muestra en los resúmenes (60, 96, 433, 915, 1088). El motor señala 'la mayoría de los resúmenes omiten el tamaño de muestra, por lo que el total verificado es sustancialmente más grande,' lo que significa que la estimación de precisión de ~2592 participantes verificados es un límite inferior y potencialmente encubre heterogeneidad en calidad o tamaño del estudio. Para inflamación (9 estudios), no se pudieron extraer tamaños de muestra de los resúmenes en absoluto, limitando la evaluación de precisión. Para función sexual, solo 1 de 3 estudios animales reporta n=35, dejando dos estudios completamente sin documentación para evaluación de rigor.

concerns.issue: Los metanálisis tienen 15–22 años de antigüedad; la base de ensayos primarios es desconocida
concerns.detail: Los tres metanálisis que agrupan evidencia humana datan de 2002, 2005 y 2007. No hay metanálisis humano más reciente ni ensayo primario presente en los registros recuperados, lo que plantea la posibilidad de que los ensayos primarios subyacentes puedan ser aún más antiguos o que evidencia más reciente no esté representada. Sin acceso a los estudios primarios citados en esos metanálisis, es imposible evaluar su calidad individual, especificidad poblacional (p. ej., solo hepatitis B/C y enfermedad hepática inducida por alcohol) o si los resultados se aplican a la salud hepática general.

concerns.issue: El resultado de inflamación carece de efecto agrupado cuantificable; la consistencia es no evaluable
concerns.detail: El resultado de inflamación está calificado como Preliminar, y el motor explícitamente señala 'no hay efecto agrupado extraíble' y 'solo un estudio humano aborda este resultado; la consistencia no puede ser evaluada entre evidencia humana independiente.' Con 8 de 9 estudios siendo modelos animales y solo 1 estudio humano sin clasificar, no hay base para inferir beneficio inflamatorio relevante en humanos, y no existe replicación para probar reproducibilidad.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo propuesto—silimarina o silibinina ejerce efectos hepatoprotectores a través de vías antioxidantes y antiinflamatorias—es plausible en células aisladas y modelos de toxicología animal (p. ej., hepatotoxicidad por aflatoxina B1 en roedores, deterioro cognitivo inducido por formaldehído). Sin embargo, hay un gran salto inferencial de modelos de lesión hepática animal a enfermedad hepática humana (hepatitis, cirrosis o salud metabólica general): los estudios animales utilizan exposición a toxinas agudas o estrés, mientras que la enfermedad hepática humana es crónica y multifactorial. La evidencia humana agrupada (metanálisis de 2002–2007) no proporciona datos mecanísticos—solo puntos finales clínicos—y el intervalo de confianza abarca cero, dejando incluso la relevancia clínica del mecanismo sin confirmar.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico argumentaría que la calificación 'Moderada' para salud hepática es exagerada: el efecto agrupado (RR 0.78 [0.53–1.15]) no es estadísticamente significativo, la base de evidencia consiste únicamente en tres metanálisis de 15–22 años de antigüedad con calidad de ensayos subyacentes desconocida, y esos metanálisis se enfocaron estrechamente en enfermedad hepática por alcohol y hepatitis viral, no en salud hepática general. Los resultados no hepáticos (cognición, función sexual, inflamación) descansan enteramente en modelos animales en conejos, caballos, roedores y aves de corral—poblaciones y modelos de enfermedad remotos del uso clínico humano—sin replicación en humanos. En conjunto, la base de evidencia no respalda afirmaciones de beneficio clínico en humanos más allá de una posible señal en una subpoblación estrecha de hepatitis/alcohol que puede estar desactualizada.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ensayo controlado aleatorizado doble ciego de alta calidad y adecuadamente potenciado (n ≥ 200) en humanos con enfermedad hepática específica (p. ej., enfermedad del hígado graso no alcohólico, hepatitis viral o lesión hepática inducida por fármacos) utilizando extracto de cardo mariano estandarizado, midiendo pruebas de función hepática y marcadores de fibrosis como resultados primarios, y publicado en los últimos 5 años, aclararía sustancialmente la eficacia humana. La replicación paralela del mismo diseño en una población independiente establecería además la reproducibilidad y aplicabilidad.
